subjects.displayTitle: Business and finance: making trust visible
subjects.introduction: A single coin earned by honest craft, Bahá’u’lláh says, is dearer to God than a treasure gathered wrongfully. From that measure flows a whole ethic of commerce: neither defraud your neighbour nor let him defraud you; allow for the profit of others and not only your own; set out each partner’s role, income and expenses so plainly that no room for dispute remains; keep a daily account book; and trade in such a way that neither profit gladdens nor loss grieves. Trustworthiness is tested first at home, with one’s own household and associates, before it can be believed in the marketplace. Leviticus had already placed honest weights and measures among the obligations owed to God, so that the ordinary tools of exchange became instruments of fidelity [1]. Business, seen this way, is a field in which trust becomes visible to everyone who deals with us. The journey continues into honesty and truthfulness as the capital no ledger records, into the status of material wealth and the distance between wealth and poverty, and into the public damage done by bribery and corruption.
subjects.arc: Begin with the worth of honest work, develop the obligations of fair dealing, and move through moderation, public integrity, and concrete accounts of commercial life.

order.why: Extend trustworthiness to a company’s protection of people’s rights.
Open with the arresting contrast between one honest coin and wrongful treasure.
Make fair dealing reciprocal: neither deceive nor accept deception.
Bring another person’s benefit into the purpose of trade.
Calls for truthfulness, sincerity, trustworthiness and fairness in commerce and every other field of work.
Translate those obligations into clear roles and agreed financial arrangements.
shortened: If a partnership is formed in commerce or in business and craft, from the beginning it should be made firm and solid. Everyone's role should be clear and evident, and income and expenses should be specified, so that there remains no room for dispute. When all accept with firm conditions and orderly arrangement, God willing no trouble will arise. Or they should not become partners from the start - each one should attend to his own work and engage in whatever is feasible, and day and night turn to God and trust in God and seek assistance and blessing from the Divine Threshold.

order.why: Test public integrity against conduct with one’s closest associates.
shortened: The friends of God must deal with each other with the utmost trustworthiness and religiosity, and whoever falls short in this regard has turned away from the counsels of the Blessed Beauty and from the divine exhortations. If a person does not deal with his household and associates with complete trustworthiness and religiosity, then no matter how honestly and faithfully he may deal with strangers, it will remain fruitless and without result. First, internal dealings must be set in order, then external matters may be addressed.

order.why: Pause over the concise call for thought and wisdom.
Consider the appeal of modest, steady enterprise.
shortened: A small business with a steady income is better than the wild, helter-skelter speculations of the financiers.

order.why: Examine the danger of allowing ambition to become greed.
Place gain and loss within the question of inward detachment.
Reflect on the relationship between honesty and customers’ trust.
Consider the public benefit of wealth rightly earned and administered.
Read an example of a company whose stated purpose includes service.
Explore mutual assistance in practical occupations.
shortened: As to helping one another, this refers to the various pursuits of life, as commerce, trade, professions, etc. In whatsoever of these a believer is in need of help, that help should be rendered.

order.why: Extend responsibility to the debts left by a deceased believer.
Turn from private dealings to the damage caused by public corruption.
shortened: As long as bribery and corruption remain the attribute of every eminent person - meaning officials and administrators - success and prosperity are impossible and unattainable.

order.why: Consider the effect of even a small unlawful gain on communal trust.
shortened: Those who are employed in government offices must conduct themselves with utmost detachment, purity, freedom, chastity and virtue, being content with their wages. They must not stain their pure garment through bribery and corruption. Today if a single soul among the friends should, God forbid, take even a penny unlawfully, the pure hem of the Cause of God would be sullied and it would bring disgrace upon all.

order.why: Complete the linked readings with the responsibility of those holding office.
shortened: And if they should commit any wrongdoing or accept any bribes, they become detested at the divine threshold and incur the wrath of the Abha Beauty, and the Truth and the people of truth become disgusted with them. Rather, they should be content with their stipend and wages, pursue the path of faithfulness, and sacrifice their lives for king and country.

order.why: Consider the hope that a partnership will become known for excellent dealings.
Retain the detailed bookkeeping example and review its supplied omissions.
shortened: Based on these proofs and evidences, it would be fitting and proper for those friends of truth to unite, all four of them, and rent a spacious shop, gathering therein whatever copper each possesses, recording in a ledger how much belongs to each, and keeping a daily account book. At the end of each month they should balance the shop's income and expenses, and spend these remaining days in the utmost joy and fragrance beneath the shadow of the Beauty of the All-Merciful, occupied day and night in remembrance of God in their hearts and souls in thanksgiving for this supreme blessing.

order.why: Consider the narrative of trust enabling a merchant to begin.
shortened: There was a Persian by the name Gassem who came from the town of Neyreez.
He was an expert tobacco-trader and anxious to settle in business.
He wished to buy 160 bales of tobacco and he did not have one cent with himself nor did he have anyone to recommend him.

When this merchant in Beirut was assured of this fact, he helped Gasem in buying tobacco and did not even ask him of his notes. Then Gasem carried the tobacco to Jerusalem where he sold it for a good profit and sent the capital to the merchant in Beirut.

order.why: Close with the story that distinguishes composure in a major loss from attention to daily expenses.

questions: What would change in a business if the rights of customers, partners, and creditors became part of its definition of success?
How do clear agreements and ordinary records express spiritual qualities, and where do good intentions need practical safeguards?
What is the relationship between careful stewardship and detachment from gain or loss in these selections?
How might the comparison with honest weights and measures help identify everyday practices that either build or quietly erode trust?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the difference between an attractive beginning and its later consequences.
Consider the prayer to practice justice and fairness as a foundation for ordinary dealings.
Reflect on the place of feasible action in pursuing a worthy purpose.

references.label: 1 · Leviticus 19:35–36
references.note: The command for honest weights and measures connects the details of exchange with fidelity to God. Compare these concrete standards with the compilation’s attention to contracts, accounts, and other people’s rights. The biblical passage belongs to Israel’s covenantal law; the comparison concerns how a spiritual obligation acquires an observable form in commercial practice.

subjects.displayTitle: Gambling and recreation: looking beyond the first moment
subjects.introduction: Not every game is suspect. Asked whether the prohibition of gambling and lotteries condemns games of every kind, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers plainly that some are innocent and harmless as pastime, and then adds the quiet caution that pastime can degenerate into waste of time. The real teaching lies in a habit of attention: the wise person, He says, looks at the consequences of a thing rather than its beginning. A cup of wine brings a moment of elation and hides the harm that follows; gambling works the same way, the thrill of the first wager concealing what it costs over months and years. Bahá’u’lláh sets the ban on gambling beside the ban on opium, within a wider care for the body and the mind. The Buddha’s discourse to Sigāla follows gambling into its six consequences, hostility, grief, loss and the wearing away of trust [1]. Recreation that truly refreshes a life asks the same discernment that alcohol and tobacco do, and finds its counterweight in useful occupation and the honest work of a trade or profession.
subjects.arc: Begin with the place of innocent recreation, look ahead to consequences, and conclude with the stated prohibition.

order.why: Start with the distinction between harmless pastime and its possible excess.
Ask the reader to look beyond immediate attraction toward consequences.
shortened: The wise person sees the consequences of matters, not their beginnings. For example, one drinks a cup of wine. Temporarily one feels elation and joy, but does not see the hangover and harm that follows. Gambling is the same way...

order.why: Retained after direct reading despite a 2.94 usefulness score: explicit, substantial prohibition of gambling alongside related practices.
Read the prohibition within this wider concern for a person’s life and well-being.

questions: What helps a person recognize when a pastime is ceasing to refresh life and beginning to consume attention, time, or relationships?
How does the Buddhist account of consequences deepen the discussion of gambling, and what does the distinction between a general rule and the judgment of particular activities bring into view?
How do the differing settings of the prohibition and the reported conversations affect what can be concluded from each?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the preference for steady work over speculative excitement.
Explore the need to bring ideals into practicable judgment.

references.label: 1 · Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta, the six consequences of gambling (Narada Thera translation)
references.note: The discourse describes gambling as a source of heedlessness and follows its effects into hostility, grief, loss, and damaged confidence in a person. Compare this attention to consequences with the selection about seeing beyond an action’s beginning. The discourse’s guidance for householders supplies its own Buddhist ethical setting; it does not define the scope of the Bahá’í law or classify every form of recreation.

subjects.displayTitle: Slavery: no servant of God is a commodity
subjects.introduction: The prohibition is short and its reason is shorter. Bahá’u’lláh forbids the buying and selling of human beings, men or women, and then gives the ground: one who is himself a servant of God has no standing to buy another of God’s servants. The ban rests not on sentiment about kind masters but on a fact about everyone, that each person already belongs to God and so cannot be anyone else’s property. That single thought has a long reach, because the same reasoning that forbids the auction block also unsettles every quieter way one person turns another into an instrument. The prayer of emancipation and the account of freedom within Bahá’u’lláh’s household give that principle a practical form, while the criticism of monuments built by enslaved people tests what a society calls greatness. Seneca, writing to a slaveholder, pleads that the enslaved breathe the same air, were born as he was and will die as he will, and asks for kindness and companionship; yet he stops at humane treatment inside the institution, where Bahá’u’lláh forbids the transaction itself [1]. The distance between those two positions is the whole question. It leads on to the oneness of humanity, and to a unity that is not a hope laid over inequality but a standing to be recognised in every servant of God.
subjects.arc: Connect prohibition and spiritual equality with emancipation, personal freedom, and the social cost of slavery.

order.why: Keep the single passage intact so that the prohibition and its reason remain inseparable.
shortened: It is forbidden you to trade in slaves, be they men or women. It is not for him who is himself a servant to buy another of God's servants, and this hath been prohibited in His Holy Tablet.

order.why: Actual act of emancipation grounded in the impossibility of one divine servant owning another.
Direct report that Baha’u’llah liberated the household’s enslaved people and allowed them to leave or remain freely.
Self-contained reported criticism of monumental building founded on the suffering of enslaved people.

questions: How does the reason given for prohibiting slavery connect spiritual equality with practical freedom?
What does the act of emancipation add to our understanding of the prohibition?
How might the account of monuments built by enslaved people change the way we evaluate a society’s achievements?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the obligation to protect people’s rights in every transaction.
Explore another statement that joins the worth of one person to that of humanity.

references.label: 1 · Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 47, §§1 and 10–13
references.note: Seneca reminds a slaveholder that enslaved people share his human origin, life, and vulnerability to fortune, and calls for kind treatment and companionship. His letter continues to address the relationship of master and slave. Place that moral appeal beside the Aqdas prohibition on buying and selling human beings, attending to the difference between recognizing humanity within an institution and forbidding the transaction itself.

subjects.displayTitle: Murder and physical harm: the worth of a single life
subjects.introduction: Whoever slays a single soul, the Báb warns the people of the Bayán, has as it were slain all mankind, and whoever gives life to one has given life to all. Everything else follows from placing one life on the scale beside humanity. Bahá’u’lláh forbids the shedding of blood in Tablet after Tablet, denies that another’s denial of God is any warrant for killing him, and declares that whoever sheds blood is not of him. Hands and tongues alike are to be restrained, and the four marks of the faithless begin with bloodshed. Yet the same Book that forbids murder provides penalties for it, death or life imprisonment, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes wilful killing from the blow never meant to kill and from pure accident, questions for a court rather than a vengeful hand. Personal restraint and public justice have to be held in view together. The Qur’án’s verse relating the life of one to the life of all stands close to the Báb’s words, and its own qualifications deserve to be read in full [1]. From here the road leads to consorting with all peoples in kindness, to the subtler harm of saddening another soul or speaking ill of them, and to the taking of one’s own life.
subjects.arc: Open with the value of one life, examine the rejection of violence and religious hostility, and then face the distinct questions of intention, defense, and public penalties.

order.why: Consider the severity of the repudiation of bloodshed.
Begin with the Báb’s image relating a single life to all humanity.
Widen the refusal of harm to hands, tongues, and hostility toward other communities.
shortened: Incline your hearts to the counsels given by the Most Exalted Pen and beware lest your hands or tongues cause harm unto anyone among mankind.

The unbelievers and the faithless have set their minds on four things: first, the shedding of blood; second, the burning of books; third, the shunning of the followers of other religions; fourth, the extermination of other communities and groups.

order.why: Connect restraint from bloodshed with the preservation of order.
shortened: Say: "Fear God and spread not disorder on earth after it hath been well-ordered, neither shed the blood of anyone, for such things are forbidden you in the Book and in this Outspread Roll."

order.why: Locate deliberate killing outside the stronghold of justice.
shortened: Say: O people, fear God and shed not blood, for this hath been forbidden by One mighty and all-knowing. Whosoever deliberately killeth a soul hath indeed departed from the stronghold of justice - thus hath the command been sent down from the realm of mighty glory.

order.why: Explains atonement and divine justice in the specific case of a murderer who has already received punishment.
Make explicit that denial of religion is no warrant for killing.
shortened: Know ye that We have forbidden the servants to shed blood and to slay those who have denied God, the Lord of lords.

order.why: Read the categorical rejection in response to a particular question.
shortened: Question: If one of the followers of the Calf, meaning one of the friends of him who turned away from God, should utter unseemly words about the Branches, and it be possible to bring him to justice in such a way that no harm would come to the Divine Cause - is this permitted or not?

Answer: This is absolutely not permitted. In all scriptures, books and tablets this reprehensible act, which is killing, has been strictly forbidden in the Book. Blessed is he who heareth! Woe to the heedless!

order.why: Attend to the repeated testimony that bloodshed was forbidden.
shortened: But observe and remember that We forbade everyone from shedding blood, as all the Tablets testify - and you are among those who know.

order.why: Reinforce the obligation to heed that prohibition.
shortened: We have forbidden the shedding of blood in most of the Tablets. Beware lest ye perpetrate what ye have been forbidden in the Book of God, the Sovereign, the Mighty, the Beautiful.

order.why: Confront the gap between the teaching and conduct that violated it.
shortened: In all the Tablets He forbade you to shed blood, yet you committed that which violated His sanctity before all creation.

order.why: Read the grouped Aqdas passages together, including their provisions for penalties.
shortened: Should anyone intentionally destroy a house by fire, him also shall ye burn; should anyone deliberately take another's life, him also shall ye put to death. Take ye hold of the precepts of God with all your strength and power, and abandon the ways of the ignorant. Should ye condemn the arsonist and the murderer to life imprisonment, it would be permissible according to the provisions of the Book.

Let none contend with another, and let no soul slay another; this, verily, is that which was forbidden you in a Book that hath lain concealed within the Tabernacle of glory. What! Would ye kill him whom God hath quickened, whom He hath endowed with spirit through a breath from Him? Grievous then would be your trespass before His throne!

order.why: Distinguish intention and accident in the account of judicial assessment.
Examine the call for fellowship with religious communities alongside the ban on killing.
Close with the supplied explanation of the alternatives for punishment, retaining its attribution.
shortened: In the Aqdas Baha'u'llah has given death as the penalty for murder. However, He has permitted life imprisonment as an alternative. Both practices would be in accordance with His Laws. Some of us may not be able to grasp the wisdom of this when it disagrees with our own limited vision; but we must accept it, knowing His Wisdom, His Mercy and His Justice are perfect and for the salvation of the entire world.

questions: What follows from seeing the life of one person in relation to the whole of humanity, especially when that person belongs to a hostile or unfamiliar group?
How do the selections distinguish restraint from harm, defense of another, and the responsibilities of a court?
What questions arise when the force of the prohibitions is read beside the passages on intention and punishment?
How does reading Qur’án 5:32 in full sharpen the comparison with the Báb’s words, and what does it suggest about the care needed when carrying a memorable passage into discussion?

neighbors.invitation: Consider a prayer for oppressors to recognize their actions and become just.
Explore the effort to replace conflict between nations with arbitration.
Attend to the people whose suffering gives urgency to the wish for peace.

references.label: 1 · Qur’án 5:32
references.note: The verse recounts an ordinance for the Children of Israel, relating the killing or saving of one person to all humanity. It includes qualifications concerning killing in retribution for a life and corruption in the land; these should remain visible in any comparison. Read the whole verse beside the Báb’s address to the people of the Bayán, considering both the shared image of human worth and the distinct wording and setting.

subjects.displayTitle: The Supreme Tribunal: making peace answerable to justice
subjects.introduction: Before any tribunal can judge between nations, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, lovers of peace must become so numerous that governments are compelled to listen; the institution rests on a public will before it rests on a treaty. From that foundation He describes the design in surprising detail: each parliament electing two or three of its wisest citizens, confirmed by senate, cabinet and sovereign so that every delegate embodies a whole nation; a court whose verdict, once given, leaves plaintiff and defendant no further pretext; and a world that rises together against any government that ignores its ruling. Shoghi Effendi sets this court within a wider commonwealth, with a legislature, an executive and a judgment binding even on parties who never agreed to appear. Kant’s distinction between a treaty that ends one war and a federation meant to end war itself sharpens the question of what such an institution must be [1]. Beyond it lie the unity of governments and the political unity of the race, the Bahá’í House of Justice as a kindred institution, and the civil courts where justice is first made answerable.
subjects.arc: Begin with the public will for peace, examine representation and the tribunal’s work, then consider enforcement, the wider commonwealth, and the limits of what the selections specify.

order.why: State the tribunal’s purpose through the prevention of war.
shortened: A Supreme Tribunal shall be established by the peoples and Governments of every nation, composed of members elected from each country and Government. The members of this Great Council shall assemble in unity. All disputes of an international character shall be submitted to this Court, its work being to arrange by arbitration everything which otherwise would be a cause of war. The mission of this Tribunal would be to prevent war.

order.why: Open with the role of people’s love of peace in making institutional change possible.
Explains the need, jurisdiction and final authority of an international tribunal to remove causes of war.
Place amicable settlement beside representation of governments and peoples.
Examine the proposed route by which representatives acquire a national mandate.
Consider wisdom and judgment as qualifications for service.
Return to the relationship between election, unity, and the prevention of war.
Ask what it means for humanity at large to protect an institution.
Develop the idea of an international court of appeal.
Distinguish the envisaged reach from the Hague tribunal mentioned in the passage.
shortened: This would be the highest court of appeal, and the parliament of man so long dreamed of by poets and idealists would be realized. Its accomplishment would be more far-reaching than the Hague tribunal.

order.why: Connect a common language with the practical work of arbitration.
Focus on the obligation to accept decisions.
Face the question of collective response to disobedience.
shortened: To remedy this condition there must be universal peace. To bring this about, a Supreme Tribunal must be established, representative of all governments and peoples; questions both national and international must be referred thereto, and all must carry out the decrees of this Tribunal. Should any government or people disobey, let the whole world arise against that government or people.

order.why: Examine the reported functions concerning boundaries, armaments, and enforcement.
Read the appeal to existing peace efforts as part of the movement toward the institution.
Retain the brief item referring to the tribunal and its details.
shortened: Fifth, universal peace among mankind, and its details. Sixth, the establishment of the Supreme Tribunal, and its details. Seventh, unity between men and women and equality of rights.

order.why: Resume with the expectation of impartial settlement.
Preserve the supplied summary and partial quotation as such.
Revisit representative selection with attention to competence and character.
Read the extended Tablet to the Hague account of election and collective backing.
shortened: And His plan is this: that the national assemblies of each country and nation--that is to say parliaments--should elect two or three persons who are the choicest of that nation, and are well informed concerning international laws and the relations between governments and aware of the essential needs of the world of humanity in this day.

The Supreme Tribunal will be composed of these people, and all mankind will thus have a share therein, for every one of these delegates is fully representative of his nation. When the Supreme Tribunal gives a ruling on any international question, either unanimously or by majority rule, there will no longer be any pretext for the plaintiff or ground of objection for the defendant. In case any of the governments or nations, in the execution of the irrefutable decision of the Supreme Tribunal, be negligent or dilatory, the rest of the nations will rise up against it, because all the governments and nations of the world are the supporters of this Supreme Tribunal.

order.why: Place binding adjudication within the proposed world political order.
Widen the view to the commonwealth’s protection of diversity and personal freedom.
shortened: The unity of the human race, as envisaged by Baha'u'llah, implies the establishment of a world commonwealth in which all nations, races, creeds and classes are closely and permanently united, and in which the autonomy of its state members and the personal freedom and initiative of the individuals that compose them are definitely and completely safeguarded.

A world executive, backed by an international Force, will carry out the decisions arrived at, and apply the laws enacted by, this world legislature, and will safeguard the organic unity of the whole commonwealth. A world tribunal will adjudicate and deliver its compulsory and final verdict in all and any disputes that may arise between the various elements constituting this universal system.

order.why: Consider the explicit clarification concerning women’s participation.
shortened: With regard to the status of women, the important point for Baha'is to remember is that in the face of the categorical pronouncements in Baha'i Scripture establishing the equality of men and women, the ineligibility of women for membership on the Universal House of Justice does not constitute evidence of the superiority of men over women. It must also be borne in mind that women are not excluded from any other international institution of the Faith.
And, there is nothing in the text to preclude the participation of women in such future international bodies as the Supreme Tribunal.

order.why: Attend to a historical use of the term in an appeal to the League of Nations.
Read the description of the League as a precursor rather than the completed institution.
Return to the proposal of collective action while preserving the supplied text’s irregularity.
Mark the acknowledged limits of foresight and the refusal to assign a date.
Retain the supplied statement about future institutional relationships for comparison with its question and context.
Close with the reminder that further elucidation and time are needed.

questions: What forms of public understanding and commitment would enable an international tribunal to be trusted as well as obeyed?
How do the proposed methods of selection connect competence, character, population, and representation, and what does the clarification about women’s participation add?
What tensions arise between national autonomy, binding decisions, and collective enforcement, and how does Kant’s federation help make those tensions clearer?
Which features of the tribunal are repeatedly affirmed, and which institutional relationships or stages of development do the selections leave for further elucidation?
How might prayer for peace and the cultivation of justice affect the conduct of the people who would build, support, or serve such an institution?

neighbors.invitation: Consider an assemblage’s prayer to become a promoter of international peace.
Explore the rejection of harm and hostility toward other religious communities.
Reflect on the claim that spiritual principle helps generate practical measures for peace.

references.label: 1 · Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace, Second Definitive Article
references.note: Kant distinguishes a treaty ending one war from a lasting league seeking to end war itself. He considers a world republic but proposes a federation as an alternative amid states’ unwillingness to accept that wider authority. Compare this reasoning with the compilation’s emphasis on binding judgments and collective enforcement. The shared aim of enduring peace does not make the institutional proposals identical.

subjects.displayTitle: Praying for justice: protection, accountability, and changed hearts
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh, seeing what has befallen His loved ones, asks God to help the oppressors achieve justice. The prayer does not stop at protection for the oppressed, though it asks for that too, for the elderly, for nursing infants, for those who bow in prayer and are shown no mercy; it asks that tyranny itself be transformed into justice, denial into acknowledgment, strangers into companions. Lament, patience, steadfastness and a demand for accountability all have their place, and the tension among them is not smoothed away. Psalm 72 opens with the same conjunction, asking that a king be given righteous judgment so that he may defend the needy and break the oppressor [1]. Princes and the learned are to be enabled to execute equity; the throne of tyranny is to be replaced by the seat of justice; the followers of every religion are to be aided toward benevolence. And the person praying is not exempt: discernment, truthful speech and fair dealing are asked for oneself. To pray this way is to begin learning fairmindedness, and to discover how justice and mercy belong to one petition.
subjects.arc: Begin with the striking prayer for an oppressor’s transformation, hear the suffering that gives it urgency, and follow the appeals into public justice and personal truthfulness.

order.why: Open with the request that oppressors become just and recognize their deeds.
shortened: Say: My God, my God! Thou seest what hath befallen Thy chosen ones and loved ones at the hands of the oppressors among Thy creatures. I beseech Thee by Thy sovereignty which hath encompassed all existence, and by Thy Name whereby Thou hast subdued both the seen and the unseen, to assist the oppressors in achieving justice and equity, and to make known to them what hath proceeded from them throughout the nights and days.

order.why: Develop the image of tyranny itself being transformed.
Connect justice with strangers becoming companions.
shortened: Manifest the effulgences of Your favors and grant justice to the oppressors. Make strangers into friends and transform others into companions.

order.why: Hear the appeal for protection of the vulnerable.
shortened: Aid the oppressed from this great injustice and protect Thy weak servants from the tyranny of the cruel ones. Thou seest, O my God, how they show no mercy even to the humble among the elderly, no compassion even to suckling infants, and spare not even those who bow down in prayer.

order.why: Attend to the prayer for patience and steadfastness amid suffering.
Bring the grief of the oppressed into the plea for the heedless to change.
Read the plea for equity from the voice of the Wronged One.
Turn toward the responsibility of rulers and learned people.
shortened: Then enable the princes of Thy earth and the learned ones of Thy lands to execute justice and equity in Thy realm. O Lord! Thou seest Thy chosen ones in the hands of the oppressors who have cast behind their backs Thy covenant and Thy testament, who have denied Thy bounty and disputed Thy signs.

order.why: Give the institutional hope a concise image: justice in the place of tyranny.
shortened: I beseech Thee to replace the throne of tyranny with the seat of justice.

order.why: Consider the need to preserve justice from oppression.
Widen the image into illumination of the earth.
Extend the petition across religious communities.
Bring justice into the practice asked of everyone.
Prays for rulers to act with justice and fairness, refrain from oppression and bring relief to their subjects.
Locate that practice in cities and regions.
Consider justice as an adornment of the people.
Connect fairness with knowledge and the removal of ignorance.
shortened: I beseech Thee, O God of existence and Master of the unseen and the seen, by Thy black tresses and Thy white hand and Thy shining brow and Thy radiant countenance and Thy Most Great Sign and the manifestations of Thy Cause in the kingdom of creation, to strip from the temples of Thy servants the garments of tyranny, ignorance and transgression, and to adorn them with the raiment of knowledge, justice and fairness.

order.why: Explore truthfulness and detachment as related qualities.
Consider the prayer for discernment of truth and falsehood.
shortened: Since you are the leaves of that tree of truth and sincerity, pray that God may guide these foolish ones and grant them insight so they may distinguish the truthful from the false and recognize friend from foe, for He says: "Whom God guides, he is rightly guided; and whom He leads astray, never will you find for him a protecting guide."

order.why: Read the direct call to fairness in responding to revelation.
shortened: Be fair in the Cause of God and His Manifestation, and be not of them who disputed His signs and denied His favor and committed that which caused every discerning scholar and every informed mystic to lament.

order.why: Ask for others to receive understanding and insight.
Make room for the personal prayer for what will truly benefit the soul.
Face the forceful appeal for judgment and removal of hatred.
Close with the supplied appeal for accountability, allowing its severity to remain part of the inquiry.
shortened: O God! Deal with their first and their last and their liars as beseemeth Thee. Verily Thou wrongest not anyone, and judgest, O my God, between all with justice, and forgivest not those who have wronged people without right. I bear witness that they have deserved what none among creation deserves. Deal with them according to what their hands have wrought in Thy path.

questions: What changes when a prayer seeks both protection for the oppressed and a change in those who oppress them?
How do petitions for patience, release, transformation, and judgment relate to one another, and where do they create difficult questions?
What might praying for justice ask of the person praying—in judgment, speech, financial dealings, or service to others?
How does Psalm 72’s focus on rulers and the needy help connect inward qualities with the public responsibilities described in this compilation?

neighbors.invitation: Explore the protection of people’s rights in an everyday institution.
Consider the relationship between deliberate killing and the abandonment of justice.
Read the same prayer for fairness together with its appeal for hearts to unite.

references.label: 1 · Psalm 72:1–4
references.note: The psalm asks God to give the king righteous judgment so that he may defend the poor and needy and confront their oppressor. Compare its conjunction of prayer and public responsibility with the petitions for rulers, the oppressed, and those who practice tyranny. The royal setting differs from many of the situations represented in the compilation, while raising a shared question about how power should serve justice.

subjects.displayTitle: Praying for peace: learning to hold the whole world in care
subjects.introduction: Console the anguished mothers, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá prays; hasten to the cry of the orphans; stay this mighty flood. Peace in these prayers has a face before it has a theory. In the dark of night He names fires kindled in valley and plain and spreading to the depths of the sea and the heights of the air, beasts trembling in their dens, suckling infants and the humble elderly and even the grazing animals in need of mercy, and then He asks something harder: that the bloodthirsty factions themselves abhor savagery and become merciful, that thoughts of hatred be turned into thoughts of love. The petition circles back on the one praying, who is to become a servant and promoter of peace, a practitioner of justice, a purifier of the heart from rancour. The Buddhist discourse on loving-kindness, extending goodwill to all beings without exclusion and asking that the recollection be kept through the day [1], widens the circle in a kindred way from a different form of address. The journey leads on to universal peace, to world unity, and to the life of prayer from which such care is drawn.
subjects.arc: Begin with those who suffer from war, widen the circle of compassion, and move toward transformed hearts, service, and the hope of a united human family.

order.why: A concise prayer for unity of hearts, guidance, love and strength to serve.
Open with the cries of children and parents affected by war.
shortened: O Lord! Come to the aid of the helpless. O Pure God! Have mercy on these orphaned children. O Self-Sufficient Lord! Stay this mighty flood. O Creator of all peoples! Extinguish this blazing fire. O Succorer! Hasten to the cry of the orphans. O True Judge! Console the anguished mothers. O All-Merciful and Compassionate One! Have mercy on the weeping eyes and burning hearts of fathers. Still this tempest and transform this world-consuming war into peace and reconciliation.

order.why: Widen the scene to the devastation of land, sea, air, and animal life.
Give voice to the prayer’s vulnerability and the image of a darkened earth.
shortened: O my Lord, my Defender, my Help in peril! Lowly do I entreat Thee, ailing do I come unto Thee to be healed, humbly do I cry out to Thee with my tongue, my soul, my spirit:
O God, my God! The gloom of night hath shrouded every region, and all the earth is shut away behind thick clouds.

order.why: Include the elderly, infants, and animals within the plea for security.
Sustain attention to creatures beyond the human community.
Ask for those engaged in bloodshed to become merciful.
shortened: We pray for all, saying: O Lord! Cause these bloodthirsty factions to abhor savagery and repent of bloodshed. Make them heavenly, divine, and merciful, that like unto angels they may become manifestations of divine virtues and daysprings of godly attributes. May they abandon differences and seek unity, be delivered from strife and conflict and pursue fellowship and concord, be rescued from the darkness of error and illumined by the light of supreme guidance.

order.why: Join the end of warfare to a transformation of thought and feeling.
shortened: Falling to the ground, I implored at the threshold of the Blessed Beauty: O Heavenly Father! Extinguish this fire and transform this war into peace. Disperse these dense clouds and illumine this dark horizon. Transform these thoughts of hatred and enmity into thoughts of love and unity, and remove this bloodshed and carnage from among Thy children.

order.why: Bring relief from torment and the restoration of ordinary life into view.
shortened: Therefore you who are the believers and the elect of God pray, pray in their behalf;- so that the conflagration set ablaze by the Kings and emperors may be extinguished, the day of Peace, good will and better things will come, the afflicted souls may be set free from the chains of slavery and torment, the world may find rest and composure and the stars of prosperity may shine and gleam.

order.why: Consider the call to keep praying while war continues.
shortened: As for you, pray meanwhile in behalf of the people--so that the forces of Peace may gain ascendance over the powers of war.

order.why: Connect peace with the ending of oppression and the establishment of fairness.
Read justice and the union of hearts in the same prayer.
Identify rancor and hatred as obstacles to unity.
Turn the petition toward service and love of all people.
shortened: O Lord! Make us brethren in Thy love, and cause us to be loving toward all Thy children. Confirm us in service to the world of humanity so that we may become the servants of Thy servants, that we may love all Thy creatures and become compassionate to all Thy people.

order.why: Extend friendship across nations and religions.
shortened: O my God! Assist Thou all of them and pour upon them the showers of Thy Supreme Confirmations; so that they may become the cause of the tranquility of the world of creation; to be the servants of the human race; to become, with all their hearts and souls, the real friends of all nations; to become with the utmost joy and fragrance, the spiritual companions of the adherents of all religions; to dispel the darkness of strangeness and to spread the lights of friendship in this transitory world!

order.why: Ask that an actual gathering become a promoter of international peace.
Remember those who serve humanity and peace.
shortened: O Lord, forgive their sins and keep them in Thy protecting shade in both worlds. O Lord, confer upon them Thy great pleasure. All are servants of international peace, all are servants of humanity.

order.why: Consider a geographically particular hope within an international aspiration.
Bring reformation of the world beside the tranquility of souls.
shortened: We beseech God to aid them all to achieve that which is conducive to the reformation of the world and the tranquility of souls.

order.why: Read the long petition that joins conduct, reconciliation, and global unity.
Pause over the concise wish for the world to be transformed.
Connect peace with tranquility and prosperity.
Imagine humanity gathered under the tents of love.
Focus on the binding together of hearts.
shortened: O God! Raise aloft the banner of the oneness of mankind and establish the Most Great Peace. Bind together the hearts.

order.why: Reach the image of the earth as one home and humanity as one family.
Resume with the humility of those asking for protection.
Close with the supplied prayer for harmony after discord and the clearing of clouds.

questions: Whose suffering becomes visible in these prayers, and how does that attention change the meaning of peace?
What does it require to pray for the transformation of people engaged in violence while also seeking protection for those they harm?
How might the Buddhist practice of extending goodwill to all beings illuminate the reach of these prayers, and how do their different forms of spiritual address remain distinct?
What actions might follow from praying to become a servant or promoter of peace, and how could those actions connect with institutions of justice?

neighbors.invitation: Remain attentive to the protection of vulnerable people amid oppression.
Explore the role of public love of peace in bringing institutions into being.
Consider the relationship between care for one life and care for humanity.

references.label: 1 · Sutta Nipāta 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta (Amaravati Sangha translation)
references.note: The discourse joins upright conduct with goodwill extended to all beings, without exclusion, and asks that this recollection be sustained in daily life. Compare its breadth of care with the prayers for humanity and other creatures. The Buddhist cultivation of loving-kindness and these petitions addressed to God have different forms, even as both invite a widening concern beyond one’s immediate circle.

subjects.displayTitle: The needs of the time: wisdom that finds a way to act
subjects.introduction: Light a candle in a gathering, not in an empty desert. With that image Bahá’u’lláh explains that observing the exigencies of the day is not a counsel of silence but of placement: purpose must find the time, the place and the listeners that can receive it. Each era has its own requirements, and time itself cannot be resisted; so the Báb spoke in terms His hearers could grasp, laws once fitting become futile when conditions change, and a once-favoured activity may later endanger the weak. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that we must speak of what is practicable, and that political affairs are left to institutions judging according to time and place. Aristotle’s account of practical wisdom, deliberating well about a good life while attending to particulars, offers a philosophical companion to this counsel [1]. Yet the Universal House of Justice warns that pragmatism alone cannot secure peace; enduring solutions arise from spiritual principle. The road ahead leads into wisdom in its deeper sense, into growth that unfolds gradually according to capacity, and toward the Manifestation of God as a physician prescribing for the needs of the age.
subjects.arc: Begin with purposeful action fitted to its setting, examine changing circumstances and concrete counsels, and conclude with the relationship between practical measures and spiritual principle.

order.why: Bring feasibility into the discussion of ideals.
Open with the candle and rain as images of purpose finding a receptive setting.
shortened: In the Holy Tablets there is mention of observing wisdom and consideration of the exigencies of place and time. By this is not meant silence, whether spiritually or earthly, but the divine purpose has been that the candle should be lit in the gathering, not in the useless desert. That the water of divine mercy may rain down on the pure land, not on the barren soil.

order.why: Join the needs of each time to steadfastness in the Cause.
shortened: Know that each day has its own requirements, each era its own characteristics, each season its own foundation, and each time its own necessities and customs. Today, the most special of deeds and most excellent of actions is steadfastness and firmness in the Cause of the All-Glorious.

order.why: Consider the force of historical change.
Attend to the capacity of an audience.
Read the relation between timing, means, and divine wisdom.
shortened: According to the exigencies of the time, means, and consummate wisdom, the outpourings of the All-Merciful from the heaven of mercy shall be bestowed, both outwardly and inwardly.

order.why: Make room for delay within the account of wisdom.
shortened: We hope that matters will be set right, and if at times there is delay, this is due to the requirements of God's consummate wisdom.

order.why: Examine the supplied account of different approaches in successive revelations.
Consider the reported explanation of social laws in their historical setting.
Explains adapting treatment and social ordinances to the differing requirements of the time.
Retain the specific reported illustration for contextual study rather than generalizing it into a historical account.
shortened: For example, it is written in the Torah that if one breaks the teeth of another, his teeth must also be broken; and if one blinds the eyes of another, his eyes must also be blinded. For the sake of one dollar the thief's hand was to be cut off. Now, can such laws be permitted and enforced in this age! Surely, no one can say it is permissible.

order.why: Explore the example concerning established habits and the timing of prohibition.
Read a particular counsel in which the requirements of wisdom affect action.
shortened: The burial of others without permission is not allowed, unless it would cause corruption. In such case, one must act according to the requirements of wisdom.

order.why: Consider the effects of public visibility in a setting of hostility.
Examine how a once-favored activity could endanger people under changed conditions.
shortened: In the early years, it was necessary to exalt the Word of God and manifest the Cause among His servants, even as the diffusion of the fragrances of the sublime Tablets and the sweet perfumes of the divine utterances were spread outwardly through messengers and inwardly through the angels brought nigh.

However, at present, the coming and going of designated souls is not viewed favorably, as it might cause perturbation in the hearts of the weak and the destruction of certain servants. Thus, from one perspective it is favored, and from another, it is not.

order.why: Explore discretion and exemption in carrying out particular ordinances.
shortened: Concerning thy question about wisdom: those ordinances which today cause the clamor of the heedless and the outcry of the ignorant must be carried out with the utmost discretion. There are many deeds that, when performed by an individual, none would be aware of them, while there are others that, when manifested, cause the opposition and objection of the heedless parties. Therefore, the Lord of Glory, exalted be His might, hath exempted His servants until such time as the Cause is made manifest through His all-prevailing sovereignty over all who are in the heavens and on earth.

order.why: Face the choice between silence and speech in a stated situation.
shortened: Today all must arise with complete dedication to promote God's Cause, but only when wisdom requireth it. In all cases, observe its requirements. For instance, silence is preferable to speech when wisdom so dictates, and likewise the reverse. In these days silence is nearer to piety, as its opposite causeth mischief.

order.why: Consider calm and steadiness in the face of opposition.
shortened: It is necessary to move with wisdom according to the requirements of the time. Today in these regions, calm, silence and steadiness are needed so the enemies may think there is nothing happening - "And they plot and God plots, and God is the best of plotters."

order.why: Attend to a specific suspension of teaching activity.
Close the linked readings with the concise reminder to observe what is wise.
shortened: Well known is it that this Wronged One loveth His friends and their presence is beloved. However, they must observe what is wise for the Cause and what the exigencies of the time require.

order.why: Distinguish inward joy from the manner of outward conduct.
shortened: The hearts must needs be filled with the utmost joy and gladness; yet outwardly regard for wisdom must be observed, and the same extreme caution as heretofore must be exercised. For the people are ignorant, indolent, unknowing, and heedless, and may imagine, God forbid, that the friends have grown remiss or deficient in their love for the Prince of the Righteous.

order.why: Consider the supplied account of institutional decisions responsive to time and place.
shortened: One hundred years ago - one ruling was necessary, today, another; tomorrow, perhaps, another. Therefore the cause of God is not rigidly circumscribed. It is in accordance with the exigencies of time and place.
Baha'u'llah says: 'Political affairs are referred to the House of Justice.' Whatever they think wise according to the requirements of time and place ought to be carried out.

order.why: Examine the expectation of renewed faith after a period of doubt.
shortened: But be not grieved, for the effulgences of the Sun of Truth shall absorb the excessive moisture of nature and shall gather together the scattered letters.
After the passing of the duration mentioned in the Book, suddenly shall the Cause of God be raised up and all souls shall turn toward it.

order.why: Consider the relation between increasing disorder and the recognition of religion’s role.
shortened: Day by day chaos and disorder in the world are increasing. Finally it will reach such a degree that human nature cannot bear it. At that time awakening will occur and souls will become aware that religion is an impregnable fortress and faith is a manifest light and divine laws, counsels and teachings are the quickener of the earth.

order.why: Read the reported narrative connecting conflict, prejudice, and a search for religion.
Question whether institutional machinery alone can secure unity.
shortened: Not even, I venture to assert, would the very act of devising the machinery required for the political and economic unification of the world -- a principle that has been increasingly advocated in recent times -- provide in itself the antidote against the poison that is steadily undermining the vigor of organized peoples and nations.

order.why: End with the explicit appeal to spiritual principle as a source of practical solutions.
shortened: ...the primary challenge in dealing with issues of peace is to raise the context to the level of principle, as distinct from pure pragmatism. For, in essence, peace stems from an inner state supported by a spiritual or moral attitude, and it is chiefly in evoking this attitude that the possibility of enduring solutions can be found.

The essential merit of spiritual principle is that it not only presents a perspective which harmonizes with that which is immanent in human nature, it also induces an attitude, a dynamic, a will, an aspiration, which facilitate the discovery and implementation of practical measures.

questions: What distinguishes fitting an action wisely to its setting from allowing convenience or fear to determine one’s purpose?
How do the selections about speech and silence change when read as counsel for particular circumstances rather than as interchangeable universal rules?
What can Aristotle’s attention to particulars contribute to the relationship between steadfast principle, experience, and judgment here?
How do the final passages challenge the assumption that workable procedures alone will produce peace, and what might a principle contribute to the discovery of a practical measure?

neighbors.invitation: Consider clear agreements as one concrete form of thoughtful action.
Examine the public conditions that make an institutional proposal practicable.
Connect spiritual aspiration with becoming a promoter of peace.

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, VI.5 and VI.7 (W. D. Ross translation)
references.note: Aristotle describes practical wisdom as sound deliberation concerning a good human life and emphasizes that action requires knowledge of particulars as well as general truths. Compare this account with the selections’ attention to time, place, capacity, and feasibility. His philosophical account and the compilation’s counsel within a life of faith have different foundations; the comparison helps ask what discerning action requires.
